sa2b42302: I wanted to recreate a childhood feeling: opening a book and wishing I could step directly into the world on its pages. The Magical Book turns that idea into an interactive web experiment connecting storytelling, generative video and spatial interaction.

s19b50860: This was never about building another history website. The goal was to test whether a browser experience could make someone feel that a physical magical book had noticed them, opened itself and become a portal.
s95fafb46: The anti-goals were written down before the first line of code: it must not feel like a landing page, a slideshow, a carousel, a video gallery, a museum information site, a dashboard, a collection of cards, an educational site with clickable pins or a standard React application. sa1bebf86: One rule mattered more than the others: civilization selection is explicit. The book never throws a visitor into a random world. It shows all ten, lets you look, and waits for a decision.
s21e744c5: Each world carries a period, a tagline, three authored discoveries and a note that the scenes are historically inspired reconstructions rather than records. Carthage was built first as the gold-standard journey and the system was then applied to the remaining nine; Ancient Egypt served as the reference clip for the depth and spatial-video research.

s8fe3c857: What if one person could delegate work to an entire AI organization?
s6f092f3b: Not a prompt, an objective. I gave an AI manager a real business question about a public marketplace, gave it an AI researcher, an accountant made of deterministic code and a memory made of PostgreSQL, and let the company run for 24 hours while I watched from a control room. This page is what actually happened, with the numbers from the run record.

sa3c1ae02: Chat AI is good at tasks: answer this, rewrite that. An organization works differently. You hand someone an outcome and they decide what to research, what to do next, when to ask for help and when the work is done. The experiment tested whether that shape could be built from agents, with one human at the top.
s65a99b05: The objective was deliberately real and measurable: a public pay-to-rank marketplace where companies bid for attention. The mission text stored in the run record asks the company to measure what every participant received relative to what they paid, identify who benefited most and least, explain why, and estimate the value captured by the platform itself.
s8ebd0639: “Measure the value every participant received relative to what they paid, and tell me what explains it.”
se99ebe21: The interesting question was never whether the model could think. It was whether the organization around it could be trusted with the result.
s22db1e8b: Five roles. Two of them are language models.
s64a638a3: “Company” is the metaphor; the architecture is smaller and stricter than the word suggests. One orchestrator decides. One researcher executes. Deterministic code owns the numbers. PostgreSQL is the only truth. The control room is a window onto it, never a source. The governing rule from the repository README: agents decide, the backend executes and records.
s22988422: The agent registry in the database holds six actors: founder (HUMAN), openclaw, grok-bot, deterministic-verifier, outbid-collector and backend (SYSTEM). There is no finance agent, no product-builder agent and no personal-assistant agent in this repository; the brief for a wider “AI company” was scoped down to what I could actually verify.
s218c4d95: The orchestrator is a plain TypeScript worker, no agent framework and no queue. It polls PostgreSQL, works out whether a decision point has arrived, and only then spends tokens. The model sees the dataset through read-only tools and can change the world through exactly one function.
